title: Terms We Choose
subtitle: Love & Duty · Chapter 11 of 40
content:
We became a polycule on a Tuesday.

Not because Tuesday was important.

Because Tuesday was the first evening all four of us were free at the same time.

That was our first lesson in romance: logistics could defeat destiny.

Aang arrived with fruit and a notebook.

Katara arrived with tea and another notebook.

Toph arrived with no notebook and immediate contempt for ours.

“If anybody makes a chart, I’m leaving.”

“You make charts with rocks,” Aang said.

“Those are tactical maps.”

“They have columns.”

“Keep talking, Twinkle Toes.”

We sat in the living room around the low table. I had expected the conversation to feel formal after all the weeks of almosts, first kisses, and careful questions.

Instead, Aang was trying to peel an orange in one unbroken spiral.

Katara kept stealing sections from him.

Toph had one foot pressed against mine beneath the table.

Somehow that made the serious part easier.

Katara opened her notebook.

Toph groaned.

“I want to start with the obvious,” Katara said. “Nobody gets to make decisions for anyone else.”

“Good,” Toph replied.

“That includes public decisions. We don’t announce anything without talking first.”

Aang nodded. “And nobody has to be equally close to everyone.”

I looked at him.

He continued, “I don’t want us turning this into a test. If two people have a difficult week, it doesn’t mean the whole relationship is failing.”

“That sounds suspiciously mature,” I said.

“I practice when you’re not around.”

Katara smiled.

Toph said, “What about sleeping?”

Aang choked on orange.

I covered my face.

Katara sighed. “Of course you went there first.”

“What? We’re talking rules.”

“We are not making a sleeping schedule tonight,” I said.

Toph leaned back. “Coward.”

Aang wiped orange juice from his hand. “We should probably talk about affection, though.”

That was how we ended up discussing things I had never imagined discussing with the Avatar over fruit.

Public hand-holding was fine for all of us.

Kisses were fine unless someone said otherwise in the moment.

Toph did not want anyone touching her feet without asking, ever, including Katara, who claimed this rule existed because of “one spa incident.”

Katara did not want arguments resolved by Aang trying to make everyone stop being angry before the anger had said what it needed to say.

Aang looked wounded.

“I don’t do that.”

Three heads turned toward him.

He sighed. “I’m working on it.”

Aang asked us not to use his role as Avatar to end personal disagreements.

“If I say something stupid,” he said, “I want you to tell me I’m being stupid. Not assume there’s some Avatar reason I’m right.”

Toph slapped the table. “Finally.”

I asked for something harder.

“If I’m upset with one of you, I don’t want the other two automatically taking sides.”

Katara’s expression sharpened with thought.

“Support without forming teams,” she said.

“Yes.”

Toph nodded. “Unless one of us is obviously being an idiot.”

“Toph.”

“What? Sometimes there’s a right side.”

Katara gave her a look.

Toph grinned.

We talked about privacy.

We talked about work.

We talked about the fact that Aang and Katara were already a long-established couple and that pretending history did not matter would be dishonest.

Katara’s fingers tightened around her cup when she said, “I don’t want either of you feeling like guests in something Aang and I own.”

I appreciated the words and distrusted how easily they could become promises no one knew how to keep.

“So what happens when history wins?” I asked.

Aang frowned. “Wins?”

“When you two have a shorthand I don’t understand. When you make a decision because you’ve always made that decision together. When Toph knows something about you from twelve years ago and I don’t.”

Toph said, “Then you ask.”

“I know.”

“No, I mean it.” Her foot pressed more firmly against mine. “You ask. We answer. If it matters, we fix it.”

Katara nodded. “And if we forget to include you, you tell us.”

“That puts the burden on me.”

The room went quiet.

Katara’s face changed first.

“You’re right.”

Aang set down the orange peel.

“We need to notice too.”

That mattered.

Not perfection.

The willingness to admit when a good-sounding rule was incomplete.

Toph tilted her head. “What about jealousy?”

Aang rubbed the back of his neck. “We haven’t really talked about that.”

“I get jealous,” Katara said.

All of us looked at her.

She frowned. “What?”

“You said it fast,” I replied.

“I know myself.”

Aang smiled carefully. “The fan club.”

Katara pointed at him. “Do not.”

Toph laughed.

Katara’s mouth twitched. “Fine. Yes. I can get jealous. It doesn’t mean anyone has done something wrong. Sometimes it means I feel insecure. Sometimes it means I want reassurance. Sometimes it means I need five minutes to stop being ridiculous.”

“That’s not ridiculous,” I said.

“Sometimes it absolutely is.”

Toph tapped her fingers on the table. “I don’t get jealous.”

Katara raised one eyebrow.

Toph scowled. “Often.”

Aang asked, “What does it feel like when you do?”

Toph shrugged.

“Like I want to punch architecture.”

“That is not specific.”

“It’s specific to me.”

I laughed.

Then Aang looked at me.

“What about you?”

I took longer.

“I think I’m less afraid of jealousy than of being temporary.”

The humor left the room.

I looked at my hands.

“You three survived a war together. You changed the world together. You have stories nobody else can enter because they already happened.”

Katara started to speak.

I held up a hand.

“I know that doesn’t mean I don’t belong. I’m saying the fear exists anyway.”

Aang moved from his cushion and sat beside me.

He did not immediately touch me.

“Thank you for telling us.”

Katara leaned forward. “I can’t give you those years.”

“I know.”

“But I can stop treating them like proof that what comes later matters less.”

Toph’s foot slid up my ankle and back down.

“You’re not temporary unless you choose to be,” she said.

It was exactly the kind of reassurance Toph could give: no promises about forever, only ownership of choice.

I breathed easier.

Aang finally took my hand.

We talked for another hour.

Children came up.

Marriage came up.

Living together came up.

Nobody decided anything.

That was deliberate.

Aang said he wanted children someday but would never treat any partner as a duty to his culture.

Katara said she wanted a family but not one built by public expectation.

Toph said children were loud, sticky, and “maybe not terrible,” which from Toph was practically a lullaby.

I said I did not know.

They let that be enough.

When the notebooks were closed, Toph immediately stole Katara’s and flipped through it.

“You made headings?”

“I like headings.”

“You made a heading called ‘conflict repair.’”

“That’s useful.”

“You’re eighty years old.”

Katara lunged for the notebook.

Toph bent the metal clasp shut.

Aang laughed.

I reached for Toph’s wrist.

She twisted away.

Within seconds the serious relationship meeting became a wrestling match over a notebook.

I ended up half across Aang’s lap, Katara had Toph around the waist, and Toph was laughing so hard she could barely threaten us.

Eventually the notebook was recovered.

We lay scattered across cushions, breathless.

Aang turned his head toward me.

“So are we calling it something?”

“The relationship?”

“Yeah.”

Toph said, “A disaster.”

Katara said, “A family.”

I looked at the three of them.

“Not yet,” I said.

Katara nodded.

No disappointment.

No pressure.

Aang squeezed my hand.

Toph’s heel bumped mine.

“What, then?” Aang asked.

I thought about four bowls on one table. Three first kisses that had felt nothing alike. Rules we would break by accident and repair on purpose.

“Us,” I said.

Toph made a face. “That’s disgustingly sentimental.”

“You love it.”

She leaned over and kissed me once, quick and firm.

“Prove it.”

Katara laughed.

Aang reached for another orange.

Tuesday ended without ceremony.

No vows. No announcement. No grand decision that love would solve everything.

Only terms we had chosen ourselves.

For the first time, that felt more romantic than destiny ever could.

We wrote the agreement down anyway.

Not because love needed a contract, but because memory became unreliable when feelings were loud. Katara kept the first copy. I kept the second. Toph refused one on principle and then made me read every line aloud so she could object to the wording.

Aang added a final sentence in the margin: We ask again when things change.

Toph ran one finger over the indentation the pen had left in the paper.

“That one stays,” she said.

So it did.

Weeks later, the paper gained coffee stains, Toph’s fingerprints, and a correction in Katara’s handwriting. It became less like a contract and more like every other important thing in our house: used, revised, and still ours.

We never treated the page as law. It was a map drawn by four people who expected themselves to change, and therefore left space in the margins for new roads.

We kept adding to it, one choice at a time.
